claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy is single-phase.
The initial alloy has a uniform elemental distribution.
The initial alloy has no pre-existing grain-boundary precipitates.
Elevated-temperature aging can produce nanoscale grain-boundary precipitates in a compositionally complex alloy.
Increasing the aging temperature from 500°C to 600°C can change approximately 5 nm discontinuous grain-boundary precipitates into an approximately 19 nm continuous network.
Prolonged exposure to 500–600°C combined with cyclic loading causes the grain-boundary precipitates to nucleate, grow, and interconnect.
Thermal aging increases atomic mobility, especially along grain boundaries.
Cyclic loading amplifies local strain and thereby accelerates grain-boundary precipitation.
A continuous grain-boundary precipitate network acts as a local stress concentrator.
The precipitate network promotes intergranular crack initiation.
A continuous grain-boundary precipitate network can cause a marked loss of ductility and brittle fracture.
Aging and cyclic loading will reduce fracture toughness relative to the as-cast alloy.
Aging and cyclic loading will cause earlier intergranular fracture relative to the as-cast alloy.
The as-cast single-phase baseline is ductile.
The as-cast baseline fails transgranularly under comparable mechanical loading.
The proposed embrittlement mechanism should dominate during long-term service at 500–600°C under repeated mechanical stress.
The same precipitate-network evolution may not occur under static isothermal exposure or at temperatures well outside 500–600°C.

contradictions.description: The boundary suggests that the same evolution may not occur under static isothermal conditions, whereas the cited precipitate dimensions and discontinuous-to-continuous transition come from isothermal aging at 500°C and 600°C without reported cyclic loading.
